2yr-02.stem: Tesla's successful entry strategy (high-end Roadster -> mass-market Model 3) fundamentally challenged the auto industry by forcing incumbents to confront which crucial strategic dilemma, according to Porter?

options.A: Whether to maximize economies of scale or economies of scope.
options.B: The trade-off between prioritizing Operational Effectiveness (OE) (efficient ICE assembly) and making radical strategic choices necessary to compete on a new basis (technology stack).
options.C: The erosion of buyer power caused by the rise of electric vehicle substitutes.
options.D: The necessity of increasing EBITDA growth to match Tesla's valuation.

2yr-02.explanation: OE vs. Strategy | Strategic success rests on value/uniqueness, which outweighs temporary OE failures when the firm’s activities are fundamentally different. |

2yr-02.stem: Tesla's deep Vertical Integration (owning battery/software IP) creates a superior barrier to imitation primarily because:

options.A: It reduces the company's reliance on external capital markets.
options.B: It forces rivals to copy the entire, complex, interwoven Activity System, making imitation structurally difficult and financially inefficient.
options.C: It guarantees flawless OE on the production floor, eliminating waste.
options.D: It ensures the company will remain profitable across all market cycles.

2yr-02.explanation: Five Forces/Vertical Integration | Vertical integration reduces supplier power by making the component (AI/Battery) a proprietary input rather than a commoditized external reliance. |

2yr-02.stem: The financial conflict associated with the SolarCity Acquisition (high cost, low immediate return) risked violating which core Porterian principle in the most severe way during the Model 3 ramp-up?

options.A: The difficulty of achieving First-Order Fit in supply chain logistics.
options.B: The necessity of making a clear Trade-off of managerial attention and capital, risking resources being diverted from the core existential mission (Model 3).
options.C: The threat of substitutes in the energy market.
options.D: The inability to benchmark core R&D effectively.

2yr-02.explanation: Third-Order Fit | Third-Order Fit optimizes effort between two distinct activities: OTA updates minimize the need for Service Centers. This synergistic link is highly defensible. |

2yr-02.stem: Which scenario best demonstrates Second-Order Fit within Tesla's Activity System?

options.A: The Cybertruck's steel exoskeleton making it cheaper to manufacture than the Model Y.
options.B: The use of Over-the-Air Software Updates to improve performance, which simultaneously reinforces the Direct Sales by centralizing the customer relationship and capturing data.
options.C: Achieving profitability in Q3 2018 after maximizing production volume.
options.D: Musk's personal brand attracting both engineering talent and retail investors.

2yr-02.explanation: Trade-off Analysis | The Trade-off was sacrificing capital (the huge cost of building the sales/service network) to gain direct control over the customer experience. |

2yr-02.stem: Tesla's Net Loss of $717.5 million in Q2 2018 (Exhibit 11a) is the direct financial consequence of which prior strategic choice and ensuing OE failure?

options.A: The cost of building the Supercharger .
options.B: The initial Trade-off to skip standard industry pilot production runs, leading to the chaotic, expensive Production Hell (OE failure).
options.C: The erosion of market share to luxury rivals.
options.D: The reduction in the Threat of New Entrants.

2yr-02.explanation: OE Limits/Convergence | Competitor success in closing the EV range gap shows that the initial technological advantage was a form of temporary OE that was eventually benchmarked, forcing Tesla to seek new positions. |

2yr-02.stem: The traditional franchised network initially represented an "insurmountable barrier" for new auto entrants. Tesla negated this barrier not by matching it, but by:

options.A: Creating an entirely new Variety-Based Positioning that targeted only non-luxury buyers.
options.B: Employing a superior Direct Sales Trade-off that was structurally incompatible with the incumbent Activity System (dealer service profits).
options.C: Outspending incumbents on national television advertising.
options.D: Achieving superior Operational Effectiveness in gasoline engine production.

2yr-02.explanation: Trade-offs | The strategic choice was to avoid the incumbent Tier 1 Supplier system, a messy Trade-off that was necessary to maintain control over Vertical Integration and IP. |

2yr-02.stem: Which of the following is the most precise Porterian definition of the long-term Strategic Position Tesla has sought since Master Plan Part I?

options.A: Cost leadership through maximizing production automation.
options.B: A focus strategy based on a unique Activity System that treats the vehicle as a vertically integrated Software Energy Platform (Variety and Needs-Based).
options.C: Access-based positioning by serving rural markets through cheap infrastructure.
options.D: Achieving Operational across all dimensions of the value chain.

2yr-02.explanation: Sustainability/Fit | The complexity of replicating the interwoven AI/Robotics Activity System creates a higher barrier to imitation than any single cost or technology. |

2yr-02.stem: In the final simulation, the primary strategic risk of choosing the Compromise option (Musk as Chairman, External CEO) is the introduction of Dissonance that threatens Fit, similar to the Yahoo case. This happens because:

options.A: The external CEO will inevitably increase R&D spending too quickly.
options.B: The two leaders’ objectives will clash: one pushing radical, high-risk Strategy, and the other demanding stable, risk-averse Operational .
options.C: The market will view the external CEO as a mere figurehead, ignoring their efforts entirely.
options.D: It triples the company’s CAPEX requirements for the Gigafactory.

2yr-02.explanation: Vertical Integration/Strategy | High R&D spending is a non-negotiable Cost of Strategy for a vertically integrated firm trying to secure a durable technological advantage. |

2yr-02.stem: Musk's intense, demanding leadership (the "super hardcore" culture) is best analyzed as a leadership style that:

options.A: Is entirely irrelevant to the competitive advantage, which relies solely on technology.
options.B: Substitutes for robust, institutionalized Operational by relying on individual and to push the radical, unproven Vertical Integration forward.
options.C: Violates the core tenet of Integration but satisfies .
options.D: Is primarily designed to reduce the of Suppliers.

2yr-02.explanation: Trade-offs/Governance | The extreme loss coupled with production issues shows the Trade-off of skipping beta testing to gain speed, which led directly to severe financial Governance Risk. |

2yr-02.stem: Tesla's low ESG Governance scores directly impact its Strategic Sustainability by:

options.A: Proving that the Model 3 assembly line is less automated than competitors' lines.
options.B: Increasing the Cost of Capital and alienating the large institutional investors needed for future growth, thereby weakening the Activity System's Fit with the financial market.
options.C: Forcing the company to abandon the Network.
options.D: Increasing the Power of Suppliers.

2yr-02.explanation: Leadership Lifecycle | The transition is needed because the founder's initial strength (chaos/vision) becomes a liability for the mature firm that requires systemic Discipline and Accountability to manage its scale. |

2yr-02.stem: The fact that the Model S outsold major luxury incumbents (Exhibit C) despite Tesla's losses (Exhibit 11a) is evidence that:

options.A: The incumbents possessed superior Operational Effectiveness (OE).
options.B: The market valued Tesla’s unique value proposition (technology and EV performance) more than OE failings in the short term.
options.C: Competitive had already occurred by 2017.
options.D: Luxury buyers are not sensitive to price or quality.

2yr-02.explanation: Fit Assessment | The synergistic link between controlling the Proprietary Software IP and maximizing the output of that IP through Direct Sales is the most powerful Fit structure. |

2yr-02.stem: Tesla’s commitment to high R&D Intensity (Exhibit A) is a clear example of Second-Order Fit because it:

options.A: Aligns with the low-cost strategy required to compete with Toyota.
options.B: Mutually reinforces the Direct Sales by consistently providing advanced software features (OTA ) that justify bypassing the dealer experience.
options.C: Reduces the of New Entrants by increasing the cost of Vertical Integration.
options.D: Is entirely driven by compliance with US .

2yr-02.explanation: Governance Objective | The core issue is whether the firm can tolerate the founder's Risk-Taking behavior given its need for Governance Checks and Balances as a mature public company. |

2yr-02.stem: Which of the following would be an example of First-Order Fit (simple consistency) in Tesla's strategy?

options.A: The founder's political opinions aligning with the company mission.
options.B: All activities, from R&D to manufacturing, being aligned with the overall goal of EV Technology Leadership.
options.C: The acquisition and Tesla creating a combined power wall product.
options.D: The company hiring a new CEO known for Operational .

2yr-02.explanation: Strategy vs. OE | The powerful unique value of the Strategic Position (the product/tech) made buyers overlook the company’s temporary OE failures (delays, losses). |

2yr-02.stem: The constant tension between Vision (Strategy) and Accountability (Governance) highlights the high organizational price of achieving a dramatic , as the successful implementation of radical strategy often requires:

options.A: The total elimination of all Integration.
options.B: A temporary tolerance for OE and that would destroy a conventionally managed firm.
options.C: A shift from Needs-Based Positioning to -Based Positioning.
options.D: The complete compliance with all rating requirements from day one.

2yr-02.explanation: Trade-offs | The compromise avoids a clear strategic choice, risking the fatal Stuck in the Middle position where the Activity System becomes incoherent. |

2yr-02.stem: Musk's dual commitments to non-Tesla ventures (SpaceX, X/Twitter) create significant strategic risk for Tesla because they:

options.A: Directly violate the Vertical Integration Trade-off.
options.B: Divert scarce Capital and Management Attention from the core Activity System, thereby imposing an external Cost that damages the firm's internal Fit and Sustainability.
options.C: Force the entire auto industry to adopt AI Robotics.
options.D: Automatically trigger a reduction in the Threat of New Entrants.

2yr-02.explanation: Third-Order Fit | OTA Updates (software) and minimizing Service Centers (physical distribution) are two separate activities coordinated to reduce redundancy, achieving optimization of effort. |

2yr-02.stem: Based on the case evidence (Zip2, X.com, Tesla), which leadership characteristic is consistently presented as both the source of Musk’s Outlier Outcomes and his greatest Governance Risk?

options.A: Extreme deference to Operational Effectiveness metrics.
options.B: Maniacal Focus and Dominance, leading to both miraculous execution and organizational burnout/conflict.
options.C: The ability to eliminate all Trade-offs.
options.D: A commitment to Variety-Based Positioning.

2yr-02.explanation: Founder's Paradox/Sociology | The extreme qualities needed to disrupt are structurally incompatible with the Discipline and Accountability required for institutional stability and OE. |

2yr-02.stem: The fundamental tension of the Leadership Lifecycle is the transition from the founder's visionary style to a professional management team. This transition is difficult because the qualities that create an Outlier Outcome (e.g., Manic Focus, Risk-Taking) are often:

options.A: Essential for generating high, repeatable EBITDA margins in a mature market.
options.B: Structurally incompatible with the Discipline, Accountability, and Institutional Fit required for long-term Governance.
options.C: Directly linked to violating the Trade-off between Direct Sales and Vertical Integration.
options.D: Only necessary during periods of low R&D spending intensity.

2yr-02.explanation: ESG/Sustainability | Low ESG scores damage the ESG profile, which increases the cost of capital and alienates institutional investors, directly threatening Sustainability. |

2yr-02.stem: The SEC charges and subsequent penalties imposed on Musk in 2018 (Case, p. 11) function as a critical Governance check which:

options.A: Primarily affected the Operational Effectiveness of the Gigafactory automation system.
options.B: Externally enforced a structural boundary on the founder's behavior, protecting the financial stability and Fit of the company for broader shareholders.
options.C: Required Tesla to abandon its Vertical Integration strategy in battery production.
options.D: Proved that Musk’s focus was entirely on SpaceX.

2yr-02.explanation: Governance/Regulatory | The SEC action was an external enforcement of Governance to protect the financial stability required for the firm's strategic Fit. |

2yr-02.stem: The SolarCity Acquisition (Case, p. 10), despite being financially disastrous and rife with conflicts of interest, had a singular strategic Defense within the context of the Master Plan, which was:

options.A: To achieve immediate economies of scale in the mass-market EV segment.
options.B: To enforce the Third-Order Fit of the Activity System by integrating the car, battery, and energy generation into one seamless platform.
options.C: To comply with the ESG requirements of the S&P 500 Index.
options.D: To eliminate the Bargaining Power of Buyers.

2yr-02.explanation: Third-Order Fit/Master Plan | The SolarCity acquisition was strategically defended as necessary to complete the Activity System by integrating the car/battery with energy generation (Third-Order Fit). |

2yr-02.stem: Musk's demand for employees to be "super hardcore" (Case, p. 7) is a management practice that directly attempts to compensate for a deficit in which area of the firm's operations?

options.A: The difficulty of making a clear Strategic Position choice.
options.B: The lack of Institutionalized Operational Effectiveness (standardized, repeatable, high-quality processes).
options.C: The limited success of the initial Roadster platform.
options.D: The inability to negotiate low prices with Tier 1 Suppliers.

2yr-02.explanation: Execution/Operational Effectiveness | The intense "super hardcore" style is a temporary, high-cost substitute for robust, repeatable Operational Effectiveness systems. |

2yr-02.stem: The Cybertruck and Optimus AI initiatives pose a high Execution Risk but are strategically necessary for Musk's retention in the CEO role because:

options.A: They are essential to maintaining the high Gross Margin of the legacy Model S.
options.B: They continuously prove that the company is still in the "Outlier Startup Phase" of the Leadership Lifecycle, justifying the founder's Risk-Taking Trade-off.
options.C: They fully automate the Fremont Factory, eliminating OE failures.
options.D: They minimize R&D Intensity below that of VW.

2yr-02.explanation: Strategic Defense/Leadership Lifecycle | Continuously pushing high-risk visions (Cybertruck, AI) is the primary way a founder justifies their retention, arguing the company is still in the revolutionary Vision phase. |

2yr-02.stem: If the Board chooses the Compromise option (Musk as Executive Chairman, operational CEO), the most significant strategic risk, based on organizational sociology and Porter's concept of Fit, is:

options.A: The new CEO will immediately reverse the Direct Sales Trade-off.
options.B: The structural division of authority (vision vs. operations) will lead to strategic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit).
options.C: The SEC will impose higher fines for inadequate Governance.
options.D: The Threat of New Entrants will dramatically increase.

2yr-02.explanation: Organizational Fit/Trade-offs | Dividing Vision (Chairman) from Execution (CEO) risks creating systemic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit), undermining organizational priorities. | |

2yr-02.stem: The Q2 2018 Net Loss of $717.5 million (Exhibit 11a), despite rising revenue, is the ultimate financial measure of the failure of:

options.A: The Third-Order Fit of the company's Activity System to eliminate redundancy in production and quality control.
options.B: The inability to increase the price of the Model 3 above $35,000.
options.C: The Trade-off associated with the SolarCity .
options.D: The Bargaining Power of Buyers.

2yr-02.explanation: OE Failure/Cost Structure | The massive Net Loss demonstrates the fundamental failure of Operational Effectiveness in production—the high costs of rework and chaos crippled profitability. | |

2yr-02.stem: Which scenario best demonstrates Second-Order Fit (where two distinct activities reinforce each other to create a unique value)?

options.A: High R&D Investment reinforces the development of Superior Battery Life, which increases the car's desirability to customers.
options.B: The use of robots to weld the chassis faster than manual laborers.
options.C: A company making the Trade-off to forgo hot meals on an airline.
options.D: The elimination of Fixed Costs in distribution.

2yr-02.explanation: Second-Order Fit | High R&D enables Superior Battery Life, which in turn reinforces the core . | |

2yr-02.stem: Tesla’s continued high R&D intensity is vital for its Strategic Position, but the persistent Governance issues (SEC, ESG) threaten its Sustainability. This paradox suggests that the firm must make a Trade-off between:

options.A: Operational Effectiveness and Strategy as mutually exclusive goals.
options.B: Radical Innovation (Strategy) and the Financial and Social Stability (Governance) needed to realize that innovation.
options.C: The Leadership Lifecycle problem and external oversight.
options.D: The Threat of Substitutes and Rivalry Among Existing Competitors.

2yr-02.explanation: Trade-off/Paradox | The paradox is the strategic Trade-off between the short-term necessity of Radical Innovation and the long-term imperative of Financial and Social Stability. | |

2yr-02.stem: If legacy automakers can achieve similar R&D levels by 2022, the most enduring non-imitable strategic difference created by Tesla's initial Trade-offs remains:

options.A: Its ability to produce the Model 3 at a lower cost than GM.
options.B: The fully integrated nature of its Activity System, particularly the relationship between Proprietary Software and the Direct Customer Relationship.
options.C: Its use of the Network, which is easily copied by utilities.
options.D: The founder's ownership stake (13%), which is irrelevant to firm operations.

2yr-02.explanation: Strategic Fit/Barriers | The combination of controlling Proprietary Software (Vertical Integration) and utilizing Direct Sales is a Fit structure that acts as a powerful barrier, as rivals cannot easily copy this interwoven system. | |

2yr-02.stem: The demand for increased voting control directly relates to the teaching objective concerning Governance and Growth because it tests the balance between:

options.A: Maximizing Operational Effectiveness (OE) versus increasing Vertical Integration.
options.B: The Vision Risk-Taking of an Outlier Leader versus the Checks and Balances needed for Sustainable Corporate Governance.
options.C: The low R&D spending of rivals versus Tesla’s high expenditure.
options.D: The Threat of Substitutes versus the Bargaining Power of Buyers.

2yr-02.explanation: Governance Objective | The 25% Control demand tests the balance between the of an Outlier Leader and the necessary Checks and Balances required for a mature public company. | |

2yr-02.stem: Exhibit 11a shows the Model S outselling major luxury incumbents (BMW 7-Series, Audi A8) by 2017. This achievement, despite Tesla's initial financial losses and quality issues (poor OE), suggests that:

options.A: Tesla had already achieved price parity with ICE vehicles.
options.B: The superior value proposition of Tesla's Strategic Position (technology/product stack) commanded sufficient Buyer Willingness to Pay to offset the functional failures in its Operational Effectiveness.
options.C: Competitors successfully imitated Tesla's Direct Sales Model immediately.
options.D: Tesla's gross profit margin remained higher than that of luxury incumbents.

2yr-02.explanation: Strategy vs. OE | The Trade-off to vertically integrate seats was driven by the need to maintain control over Quality and Design to reinforce the Position, despite the higher OE costs of not outsourcing. | |

2yr-02.stem: Choosing to RETAIN MUSK as CEO in the simulation (Option A) is fundamentally based on accepting the high cost of the Founder's Paradox because it prioritizes the teaching objective of:

options.A: Evaluating the optimal management needed for predictable quarterly earnings (OE).
options.B: Analyzing how an individual leader can make a difference revolutionizing a whole industry, viewing the chaos as a necessary byproduct of Risk-taking (Case, p. 2).
options.C: Reflecting on the need for strong Corporate Governance principles (ESG Index).
options.D: Proving that the company has completed the Leadership Lifecycle transition.

2yr-02.explanation: Strategy vs. OE | The Model S's continued sales success despite poor OE (losses, delays) proves that the unique value of the firm's Strategic Position Trumps the temporary failings of its Operational Effectiveness. | |

2yr-02.stem: Musk's commitments to non-Tesla ventures (SpaceX, X/Twitter) create significant strategic risk for Tesla because they:

options.A: Directly violate the Vertical Integration Trade-off.
options.B: Divert scarce Capital and Management Attention from the core Activity System, thereby imposing an external Cost that damages the firm's Fit and Sustainability.
options.C: Force the entire auto industry to adopt AI Robotics.
options.D: Automatically trigger a reduction in the Threat of New Entrants.

2yr-02.explanation: Resource/Fit Cost | External commitments divert scarce Capital and Management Attention (resources) from the core Tesla Activity System, imposing an external Cost that directly damages the firm's internal Fit and Sustainability. | |

options.C: Directly linked to violating the Trade-off between Direct Sales and Vertical Integration.
options.D: Only necessary during periods of low R&D spending intensity.

1yr-02.explanation: ESG/Sustainability | Low ESG scores damage the ESG profile, which increases the cost of capital and alienates institutional investors, directly threatening Sustainability. |

1yr-02.stem: The SEC charges and subsequent penalties imposed on Musk in 2018 (Case, p. 11) function as a critical Governance check which:

options.A: Primarily affected the Operational Effectiveness of the Gigafactory automation system.
options.B: Externally enforced a structural boundary on the founder's behavior, protecting the financial stability and Fit of the company for broader shareholders.
options.C: Required Tesla to abandon its Vertical Integration strategy in battery production.
options.D: Proved that Musk’s focus was entirely on SpaceX.

1yr-02.explanation: Governance/Regulatory | The SEC action was an external enforcement of Governance to protect the financial stability required for the firm's strategic Fit. |

1yr-02.stem: The SolarCity Acquisition (Case, p. 10), despite being financially disastrous and rife with conflicts of interest, had a singular strategic Defense within the context of the Master Plan, which was:

options.A: To achieve immediate economies of scale in the mass-market EV segment.
options.B: To enforce the Third-Order Fit of the Activity System by integrating the car, battery, and energy generation into one seamless platform.
options.C: To comply with the ESG requirements of the S&P 500 Index.
options.D: To eliminate the Bargaining Power of Buyers.

1yr-02.explanation: Third-Order Fit/Master Plan | The SolarCity acquisition was strategically defended as necessary to complete the Activity System by integrating the car/battery with energy generation (Third-Order Fit). |

1yr-02.stem: Musk's demand for employees to be "super hardcore" (Case, p. 7) is a management practice that directly attempts to compensate for a deficit in which area of the firm's operations?

options.A: The difficulty of making a clear Strategic Position choice.
options.B: The lack of Institutionalized Operational Effectiveness (standardized, repeatable, high-quality processes).
options.C: The limited success of the initial Roadster platform.
options.D: The inability to negotiate low prices with Tier 1 Suppliers.

1yr-02.explanation: Execution/Operational Effectiveness | The intense "super hardcore" style is a temporary, high-cost substitute for robust, repeatable Operational Effectiveness systems. |

1yr-02.stem: The Cybertruck and Optimus AI initiatives pose a high Execution Risk but are strategically necessary for Musk's retention in the CEO role because:

options.A: They are essential to maintaining the high Gross Margin of the legacy Model S.
options.B: They continuously prove that the company is still in the "Outlier Startup Phase" of the Leadership Lifecycle, justifying the founder's Risk-Taking Trade-off.
options.C: They fully automate the Fremont Factory, eliminating OE failures.
options.D: They minimize R&D Intensity below that of VW.

1yr-02.explanation: Strategic Defense/Leadership Lifecycle | Continuously pushing high-risk visions (Cybertruck, AI) is the primary way a founder justifies their retention, arguing the company is still in the revolutionary Vision phase. |

1yr-02.stem: If the Board chooses the Compromise option (Musk as Executive Chairman, operational CEO), the most significant strategic risk, based on organizational sociology and Porter's concept of Fit, is:

options.A: The new CEO will immediately reverse the Direct Sales Trade-off.
options.B: The structural division of authority (vision vs. operations) will lead to strategic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit).
options.C: The SEC will impose higher fines for inadequate Governance.
options.D: The Threat of New Entrants will dramatically increase.

1yr-02.explanation: Organizational Fit/Trade-offs | Dividing Vision (Chairman) from Execution (CEO) risks creating systemic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit), undermining organizational priorities. | |

1yr-02.stem: The Q2 2018 Net Loss of $717.5 million (Exhibit 11a), despite rising revenue, is the ultimate financial measure of the failure of:

options.A: The Third-Order Fit of the company's Activity System to eliminate redundancy in production and quality control.
options.B: The inability to increase the price of the Model 3 above $35,000.
options.C: The Trade-off associated with the SolarCity .
options.D: The Bargaining Power of Buyers.

1yr-02.explanation: OE Failure/Cost Structure | The massive Net Loss demonstrates the fundamental failure of Operational Effectiveness in production—the high costs of rework and chaos crippled profitability. | |

1yr-02.stem: Which scenario best demonstrates Second-Order Fit (where two distinct activities reinforce each other to create a unique value)?

options.A: High R&D Investment reinforces the development of Superior Battery Life, which increases the car's desirability to customers.
options.B: The use of robots to weld the chassis faster than manual laborers.
options.C: A company making the Trade-off to forgo hot meals on an airline.
options.D: The elimination of Fixed Costs in distribution.

1yr-02.explanation: Second-Order Fit | High R&D enables Superior Battery Life, which in turn reinforces the core . | |

1yr-02.stem: Tesla’s continued high R&D intensity is vital for its Strategic Position, but the persistent Governance issues (SEC, ESG) threaten its Sustainability. This paradox suggests that the firm must make a Trade-off between:

options.A: Operational Effectiveness and Strategy as mutually exclusive goals.
options.B: Radical Innovation (Strategy) and the Financial and Social Stability (Governance) needed to realize that innovation.
options.C: The Leadership Lifecycle problem and external oversight.
options.D: The Threat of Substitutes and Rivalry Among Existing Competitors.

1yr-02.explanation: Trade-off/Paradox | The paradox is the strategic Trade-off between the short-term necessity of Radical Innovation and the long-term imperative of Financial and Social Stability. | |

1yr-02.stem: If legacy automakers can achieve similar R&D levels by 2022, the most enduring non-imitable strategic difference created by Tesla's initial Trade-offs remains:

options.A: Its ability to produce the Model 3 at a lower cost than GM.
options.B: The fully integrated nature of its Activity System, particularly the relationship between Proprietary Software and the Direct Customer Relationship.
options.C: Its use of the Network, which is easily copied by utilities.
options.D: The founder's ownership stake (13%), which is irrelevant to firm operations.

1yr-02.explanation: Strategic Fit/Barriers | The combination of controlling Proprietary Software (Vertical Integration) and utilizing Direct Sales is a Fit structure that acts as a powerful barrier, as rivals cannot easily copy this interwoven system. | |

1yr-02.stem: The demand for increased voting control directly relates to the teaching objective concerning Governance and Growth because it tests the balance between:

options.A: Maximizing Operational Effectiveness (OE) versus increasing Vertical Integration.
options.B: The Vision Risk-Taking of an Outlier Leader versus the Checks and Balances needed for Sustainable Corporate Governance.
options.C: The low R&D spending of rivals versus Tesla’s high expenditure.
options.D: The Threat of Substitutes versus the Bargaining Power of Buyers.

1yr-02.explanation: Governance Objective | The 25% Control demand tests the balance between the of an Outlier Leader and the necessary Checks and Balances required for a mature public company. | |

1yr-02.stem: Exhibit 11a shows the Model S outselling major luxury incumbents (BMW 7-Series, Audi A8) by 2017. This achievement, despite Tesla's initial financial losses and quality issues (poor OE), suggests that:

options.A: Tesla had already achieved price parity with ICE vehicles.
options.B: The superior value proposition of Tesla's Strategic Position (technology/product stack) commanded sufficient Buyer Willingness to Pay to offset the functional failures in its Operational Effectiveness.
options.C: Competitors successfully imitated Tesla's Direct Sales Model immediately.
options.D: Tesla's gross profit margin remained higher than that of luxury incumbents.

1yr-02.explanation: Strategy vs. OE | The Trade-off to vertically integrate seats was driven by the need to maintain control over Quality and Design to reinforce the Position, despite the higher OE costs of not outsourcing. | |

1yr-02.stem: Choosing to RETAIN MUSK as CEO in the simulation (Option A) is fundamentally based on accepting the high cost of the Founder's Paradox because it prioritizes the teaching objective of:

options.A: Evaluating the optimal management needed for predictable quarterly earnings (OE).
options.B: Analyzing how an individual leader can make a difference revolutionizing a whole industry, viewing the chaos as a necessary byproduct of Risk-taking (Case, p. 2).
options.C: Reflecting on the need for strong Corporate Governance principles (ESG Index).
options.D: Proving that the company has completed the Leadership Lifecycle transition.

1yr-02.explanation: Strategy vs. OE | The Model S's continued sales success despite poor OE (losses, delays) proves that the unique value of the firm's Strategic Position Trumps the temporary failings of its Operational Effectiveness. | |

1yr-02.stem: Musk's commitments to non-Tesla ventures (SpaceX, X/Twitter) create significant strategic risk for Tesla because they:

options.A: Directly violate the Vertical Integration Trade-off.
options.B: Divert scarce Capital and Management Attention from the core Activity System, thereby imposing an external Cost that damages the firm's Fit and Sustainability.
options.C: Force the entire auto industry to adopt AI Robotics.
options.D: Automatically trigger a reduction in the Threat of New Entrants.

1yr-02.explanation: Resource/Fit Cost | External commitments divert scarce Capital and Management Attention (resources) from the core Tesla Activity System, imposing an external Cost that directly damages the firm's internal Fit and Sustainability. | |
